analysis.one_liner: Caps shipping rates between the mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico at near international-market levels.
analysis.headline: The bill drew zero cosponsors, never received a committee or floor vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a benchmark into law for ocean shipping rates on routes between the US mainland and Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other noncontiguous areas. A rate would count as "reasonable" only if it fell within 10 percent of a rate set by an international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission. These routes are served by a small set of US-flag carriers under the Jones Act, and households and businesses in the islands pay shipping costs far above international norms. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: Households and businesses in Hawaii, Alaska, Puerto Rico, and other noncontiguous areas, who pay elevated prices for shipped goods because the Jones Act restricts these routes to a small group of US-flag carriers; if rates were pegged to an international index, some of that premium could shrink or grow more slowly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents of Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico

how_it_helps.text: The bill would amend federal law so that a rate in the noncontiguous domestic ocean trade is reasonable only if it is within 10 percent of a rate set by a comparable international ocean rate index recognized by the Federal Maritime Commission.
The bill amends Section 13701(d) of title 49, United States Code, which governs the reasonableness of rates in this trade, replacing the existing general standard with the index-based test.

analysis.who_pays: The handful of carriers operating US-flag service between the mainland and the noncontiguous states and territories, whose rates currently face only a general reasonableness standard and often run above international index levels.

drawbacks.text: Carriers in this trade operate under the Jones Act, which requires US-built, US-crewed vessels that cost far more to build and operate than foreign ships, so a rate pegged to an international index could fall below the carriers' actual cost of service and discourage investment in the US-flag fleet.

The standard depends on the Federal Maritime Commission "recognizing" a comparable international rate index, a vague test that could invite litigation and leave both shippers and carriers uncertain about what rates are lawful.
If the cap squeezed carriers out of some routes, island communities could face reduced service frequency, which for them could be worse than paying higher rates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: island residents pay some of the highest shipping-driven price premiums in the country, and the bill would give regulators a concrete yardstick instead of an open-ended reasonableness test. But the design is crude. International index rates do not reflect the higher costs of US-built, US-crewed vessels, and a rigid 10 percent band could undermine the financial case for serving these routes at all. A better-designed version would pair a rate benchmark with a service guarantee or a cost study; this bill offered the benchmark alone.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee where it stayed until the two-year Congress ended; it never got a hearing, a vote, or a cosponsor.

narrative.text: Representative Ed Case of Hawaii introduced the bill on January 13, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the same day.
On February 4, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two-year life.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the bill ever receiving a markup or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The carriers serving the noncontiguous trade are better off, since rates on these routes remain governed only by the general reasonableness standard and stay untethered from international index levels. Island consumers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Jones Act carriers serving the island routes

for.name: Rep. Ed Case
for.role: U.S. Representative for Hawaii and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and made introductory remarks on the House floor; no colleague joined him as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Peter DeFazio (D)
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or scheduled the bill for consideration in the two years after referral, routing it to a subcommittee where it stalled.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition cannot be measured.

industries.industry: Jones Act carriers in the noncontiguous domestic trade (e.g., Matson, Pasha, TOTE, Crowley)
industries.note: The bill would cap the rates these carriers can charge on routes to Hawaii, Alaska, and Puerto Rico at roughly international-index levels, directly limiting the premium rates the trade currently supports. Their interest in blocking the bill runs against island consumers, who absorb those premium rates in the price of nearly everything they buy.

industries.industry: US shipyards and US-flag maritime operations
industries.note: By pegging rates to international indexes that do not reflect the cost of US-built, US-crewed ships, the bill could weaken the financial case for maintaining and building US-flag vessels. Consumers on the islands would pay less, but the domestic fleet that serves them could shrink.
